power.title: Where the power comes from, and who pays
paragraphs: A data center doesn't have its own private power plant (with rare exceptions). It draws from the same regional grid as every home: power plants generate electricity, high-voltage transmission lines carry it long distances, substations step the voltage down, and distribution lines deliver it to buildings. The difference is scale: a large data center connects directly to transmission through its own dedicated substation, which the data center pays to build.

How big is the load, honestly? In 2023, all U.S. data centers together used about 4.4% of the nation's electricity (a measured federal estimate). Government and independent projections put that at roughly 9-17% by 2030, but those are models, not measurements, and they disagree because nobody knows how fast AI demand will really grow. A 100 MW campus running near-continuously uses about as much electricity as 65,000-81,000 homes. That comparison is fair for volume but misleading in one way: data centers draw power steadily around the clock, while homes spike at dinnertime; steady load is actually easier for a grid to plan around, if there's time to build for it.

The real source of grid stress is a timing mismatch: a data center is built in 18-24 months, but transmission upgrades take 7-10 years. Utilities manage the gap by phasing ramp-ups, requiring developers to fund upgrades, and screening out speculative projects; they receive an estimated 5-10x more connection requests than facilities actually built.

Who pays for the wires? Interconnection rules split costs into two buckets. Dedicated equipment serving only the facility (substation bays, transformers, tap lines) is paid by the data center, full stop. 'Network upgrades' that strengthen the shared grid are traditionally spread across all customers, and that second bucket is where cost-shifting happens and where states are rewriting rules: Ohio now makes large data centers pay at least 85% of contracted capacity whether used or not; Virginia's new rate class requires 14-year contracts; Georgia requires minimum billing and regulator review of large contracts.

So will bills go up? Both answers are true, under different conditions. Looking backward, the best national causal study found data center growth from 2019-2024 actually lowered average residential rates slightly; more sales spread the grid's fixed costs. Looking forward, peer-reviewed models project increases of 6-29% nationally by 2030 if new supply can't keep pace. Both can be right: the rate-lowering effect only works when new power plants can be built cheaply and quickly. Where supply is constrained, new demand bids up scarce capacity. This is already visible in the PJM region, where capacity prices hit records and the independent market monitor attributes roughly 40% of recent auction costs to data center demand.

What can you actually check? The large-load tariff and the facility's service agreement are filed at your state Public Utility Commission; the System Impact Study lists exactly which upgrades are needed and who pays; grid operators publish real-time fuel mix and reserve margins. The right question at a hearing is not 'will rates go up?' but 'does this facility have a minimum-take contract, for how many years, and which upgrade costs are in the shared bucket?'

water.title: Water use is a design choice, not a fixed property
paragraphs: Two data centers of identical size can differ in water use by a factor of 100. A facility with evaporative cooling towers sprays water over heat exchangers and loses most of it to evaporation; in a hot, dry summer, that can be up to roughly 9 liters for every kilowatt-hour the servers use. A facility with closed-loop liquid cooling is filled once, like a car radiator, and consumes almost nothing afterward. The honest answer to 'how much water?' is: read the cooling section of the site plan, not the words 'data center.'

The size ladder, with benchmarks: a medium evaporatively cooled data center can use up to ~300,000 gallons a day, about what 1,000 average American homes use (EPA: a family uses 300+ gallons/day). The largest campuses can reach millions of gallons a day. But an air-cooled facility of the same computing power sits near the bottom of that ladder, closer to a large office building.

Where does the water actually go? In evaporative systems, about 80% evaporates into the sky and leaves the watershed; about 20% is discharged as mineral-concentrated 'blowdown' to the sewer. That is different from home use, where most water returns to treatment plants, which is why utilities count data center water as 'consumptive' use.

The hidden half: electricity is water. Nationally, the water consumed at power plants to generate data centers' electricity was about 12 times what data centers used onsite in 2023. An 'air-cooled, waterless' facility still has a water footprint; it just shows up at the power plant, and it grows because air cooling takes more energy. Whether that matters locally depends on your regional grid mix.

Wells and aquifers: most large data centers buy treated municipal water, which means they generally cannot pump your well dry, but they can strain a shared municipal system, and heavy construction near shallow wells has coincided with sediment and dry taps in Newton County, Georgia (causation there is disputed). Where facilities do drill their own wells, the questions that matter are which aquifer, how deep, how much, and what the aquifer's safe yield is. St. Joseph County, Indiana answered them publicly by capping industrial use at about half the aquifer's estimated safe yield.

Trust and verify: industry surveys found fewer than a third of operators even tracked water use, and in The Dalles, Oregon it took a 13-month legal fight before records showed Google's campuses used 29% of the city's water. Things are improving (Google now reports annual consumption; Microsoft publishes fleet WUE), but these are company-reported numbers. Communities can require stronger terms: gallons-per-day caps, WUE disclosure, baseline well testing, and public meter reporting written into the development agreement.

noise.title: What the hum is, and how to hold anyone to a number
paragraphs: A data center's noise does not come from computers; it comes from the equipment that keeps them cool and powered. The main sources are cooling fans and chillers (a steady whoosh or hum, running 24/7), transformers (a constant electrical hum), and backup generators (very loud, but only during short scheduled tests and outages). In documented cases, unmitigated cooling equipment has produced 45-65 dBA at the property line around the clock, and generator tests reach 90-105 dBA up close.

How loudness is measured, and why 'dBA' doesn't tell the whole story. Most rules use dBA, a scale tuned to how ears hear mid-range sounds like speech. But the most annoying part of data center noise is often a low-frequency hum or a persistent tone, and dBA partially filters those out. That is why a facility can technically 'meet code' while neighbors still hear (or feel) a hum indoors at night. A second scale, dBC, captures low frequencies; a big gap between a facility's dBC and dBA readings is a red flag. Modern ordinances increasingly add dBC or frequency-band limits for exactly this reason.

How sound fades: from a compact source like a chiller yard, sound drops about 6 dB every time you double your distance: equipment producing 70 dBA at 50 feet is roughly 58 dBA at 200 feet and 46 dBA at 800 feet under ideal conditions. Two caveats: a 3 dB change is barely noticeable (it takes about 10 dB to sound 'half as loud'), and low-frequency hum fades more slowly, especially on still nights.

What went wrong in real communities: Chandler, Arizona residents lived next to a data center hum for years starting around 2014; retrofitted acoustic blankets and screen walls helped but never fully fixed it. Prince William County's old noise rules exempted cooling equipment entirely. Lawsuits filed in 2026 in Michigan and Wisconsin allege continuous hum audible far from the fence line. The pattern in every failure: loud equipment close to homes, no enforceable number in the approval, and mitigation attempted only after people were already suffering.

What works is engineering, decided before construction: distance (setbacks measured from equipment, not just buildings), quiet-by-design equipment (low-speed fans, enclosed chillers, closed-loop cooling), orienting mechanical yards away from homes, and acoustic barriers or berms, which can cut 5-10 dB or more, but only if they block the line of sight and the equipment isn't on a roof above them. Because retrofits only partially worked in Chandler, the strongest protection is designing quiet from the start against a hard number.

How to hold anyone to it: a noise promise is only real if it appears in the permit as a measurable limit at the property line, ideally with both dBA and dBC numbers, a pre-construction baseline study, compliance testing before opening, and penalties. Spotsylvania County, Virginia shows this is achievable: every approved data center there committed to a 55-65 dBA property-line maximum, with developer-funded compliance testing required before occupancy and permit revocation available for repeat violations. These conditions are public documents; you can read them yourself.

taxes.title: Where the money actually comes from (hint: it's the servers, not the land)
paragraphs: A data center building pays real property tax like any warehouse, but in states like Virginia, the far bigger check is the tax on the computer equipment inside. Loudoun County taxes servers at $4.15 per $100 of value versus $0.805 for real estate, and that equipment tax brought in about $795 million in one budget year, roughly 40% of the county's entire local tax funding. Whether your state taxes equipment at all is the single biggest factor in what your community would receive.

What a 'tax break' actually is: most data center incentives are state sales-tax exemptions on server purchases; Virginia's was worth $929 million in FY23, its largest economic development incentive. Local abatements (reducing property tax for a set period) and PILOTs (negotiated payments in lieu of taxes) are separate, local decisions. An abatement doesn't mean zero payment (New Albany, Ohio pairs abatements with community-authority charges, income tax, and PILOT backstops), but it does mean the headline number isn't what schools and the county will see during the abatement years.

The disclosure problem: only 11 states disclose which companies receive data center subsidies; 24+, including Virginia and Georgia, do not. Almost no state tracks whether promised jobs actually materialized, and states that studied returns found they lose 52-70 cents per subsidy dollar. Whatever you think of the tradeoff, residents can't evaluate a deal they can't see, which is why requiring published agreements is a reasonable, non-partisan ask.

The depreciation cliff: equipment revenue is only durable if servers keep getting replaced. Assessments start around 50% of purchase price and fall fast; when refresh cycles slowed in 2021, Loudoun missed its forecast by $60 million. A county budgeting data center revenue as a permanent flat stream is making a bet on refresh cycles; good budget practice treats it as volatile and avoids over-dependence.

How to verify all of this yourself: your county's adopted budget is public: search it for 'business personal property' or 'computer equipment' line items and the tax rate schedule. Ask the commissioner of revenue for the depreciation schedule, the planning office for any abatement or CBA documents, and read both Virginia's JLARC report and Good Jobs First's subsidy reports, the same public documents read from opposite perspectives, which is exactly why you should read both.

jobs.title: The honest jobs numbers: headcount, the full role spectrum, and round-the-clock staffing
paragraphs: A typical single data center building employs about 50 permanent workers, and independent research comparing counties that got data centers with counties whose projects were canceled finds roughly 100-200 net new jobs over a decade. The larger employment event is construction: up to 1,500 workers at peak on one building, and about 59,000 of the 74,000 jobs Virginia's audit attributes to the industry are construction-phase. Data centers are a tax-revenue story more than a headcount story, and both sides of that deserve to be stated plainly.

What the jobs pay is often understated. The widely quoted $54,000 figure is the national average for the entry-level technician title on job-posting aggregators. The actual role spectrum at and around data centers runs much higher: senior and critical-facilities technicians ($80k-$130k+), facility managers (about $145k average total pay, self-reported data), and, per federal wage statistics, mechanical engineers ($102k median), electrical engineers ($112k), network administrators ($97k), information security analysts ($125k), computer network architects ($130k), and database architects ($136k). Certified cybersecurity professionals average $147k in ISC2's workforce survey. At major tech employers, senior through principal engineers report median total compensation of roughly $312k to $551k including equity; those packages concentrate at hyperscaler hub locations rather than every campus, and the equity component moves with stock prices. The full matrix with sources is below.

Round-the-clock operation shapes the headcount. Staffed data centers keep people on site 24/7/365: operations guidance calls for at least 1-2 qualified operators on site at all times at high-tier facilities, and critical-facilities technicians, network operations centers, and security are typical continuous posts at larger campuses. Standard workforce arithmetic says each continuously staffed seat consumes roughly 4.2-5.4 full-time employees once shifts, leave, and training are covered. Two consequences: published per-facility figures like JLARC's ~50 are total headcount across all shifts (they should not be multiplied by a shift ratio), and a 50-person facility supports only about 9-12 concurrent 24/7 seats, which is why large multi-building campuses running on-site NOC and SOC operations carry headcounts in the hundreds.

About 'thousands of jobs supported' claims: big totals usually come from input-output models that add indirect and induced jobs, which are modeled ripple effects rather than people badging into the facility. Independent studies consistently find smaller net effects than industry-commissioned ones, and subsidy critics calculate some deals cost $1-2 million per permanent job. Ask which number is direct, on-site, permanent headcount, and which is modeled.

How to verify job commitments: get direct-FTE commitments in writing, check state incentive filings for minimum job and wage requirements (Virginia's exemption requires 150% of prevailing wage), and read local-hiring language carefully: 'good faith efforts' is a goal, not a guarantee. Funded training before operations begin, like community college partnerships, is the strongest signal that local residents will fill the roles.

property.title: Data Centers and Your Home's Value: What the Evidence Actually Shows
paragraphs: The honest answer is that the evidence is mixed, and anyone who tells you data centers definitely raise or definitely crash home values is overselling. The most rigorous national study, from the Brookings Institution, compared counties that got data centers with counties where projects were canceled and found home prices rose a modest 2-5%, but that is a county-wide average, not a promise about the house across the street from the cooling yard.

Studies of the most data center-dense place on Earth (Northern Virginia) found no statistical evidence that proximity hurts home values; homes closer to data centers actually sold for more. But the George Mason researchers themselves warn this is because data centers locate near good roads, utilities, and jobs that buyers also want. Realtor.com's national comparison of 43 ZIP codes that gained facilities found values simply tracked similar neighborhoods without them.

On the other side: an industry-commissioned Indiana appraisal that headlined 'no adverse effect' actually showed homes near facilities in three of four counties appreciating 1-9% less than county averages. Real estate agents report hard-to-sell listings near proposed sites, and one Texas community saw prices fall 8.2% in a year, though that drop may reflect the broader market. What seems to matter most is distance, direct visibility, noise and light at your property line, and whether your market is hot or cooling.

How to verify: read the Brookings, GMU, and Realtor.com studies yourself (they're free), ask who paid for any study presented at a zoning hearing, and pull actual sale records from your county assessor for streets next to existing facilities in towns like yours, not blended county averages.

construction.title: The Construction Years: What to Expect and How to Hold Builders Accountable
paragraphs: A single data center building typically takes 18 to 36 months to build, but that number can mislead: large campuses are built in phases, so communities near multi-building sites should expect rolling construction (grading, concrete pours, steel, and fit-out) for five years or more. The loudest, dustiest, most truck-heavy period is the first year of earthmoving and foundations.

The workforce is real and temporary. Academic benchmarks put peak staffing at roughly 0.7 to 2 construction workers per megawatt: over a thousand workers for a big hyperscale building, and up to 5,000 at giant campuses like Meta's in Louisiana, where RV camps, pre-dawn truck convoys, and rent spikes followed. In small towns, worker housing pressure can be as disruptive as the trucks.

The complaints are documented, not hypothetical: a Virginia homeowner is suing Amazon over months of dust, brown well water, late-night noise, and foundation vibration during construction; Michigan residents documented speeding gravel trucks tearing up freshly paved streets. The difference between a hard couple of years and a nightmare is usually a written construction management plan: set work hours, designated haul routes, dust watering, street sweeping, a complaint hotline with response deadlines, and penalties for violations.

How to verify: before approval, ask your planning department whether the construction management plan, traffic study, and complaint process are binding conditions of approval. During construction, log complaints in writing through the official channel; documented complaints created the enforcement record in every case above.

landuse.title: Why Here? Land, Siting, and What Happens When the Servers Leave
paragraphs: Data centers chase four things: electric capacity (big developers now look for sites that can reach 300+ megawatts), fiber optic routes, large affordable parcels, and permissive zoning. That formula is why flat farmland near a substation or transmission line, not a downtown lot, keeps getting picked, and why new facilities are moving to cheaper land in lower-income areas farther from cities. If your community is asking 'why us,' the answer is usually visible on a utility map.

The land trade-off is real. Roughly 4,900 facilities are built or underway nationally, and the American Farm Bureau warns that farmland conversion is effectively permanent; hundreds of acres of impermeable roof and pavement don't go back to corn. Job density is also low for the acreage: one Northern Virginia campus that held 5,300 office jobs was replaced by data centers employing about 100 to 150 people.

The harder question is the exit. Server halls are purpose-built, hard to reuse, and the technology inside turns over every five to ten years. Unlike solar farms, where decommissioning bonds are standard, most jurisdictions require nothing if a data center operator walks away. That is starting to change: two Pennsylvania townships now mandate decommissioning within 12 months including hazardous-material removal, and Ohio requires large data centers with weak credit to post financial assurances so ratepayers aren't stuck with stranded grid upgrades.

How to verify: ask whether your project's approval includes a decommissioning plan and a bond or letter of credit sized to actual demolition cost; ask which brownfield alternatives were considered; and check the utility's public interconnection queue to understand what grid capacity the site was chosen for.

safety.title: Fuel, Batteries, and Fire Trucks: The Real Safety Picture
paragraphs: Data centers are quiet neighbors most of the time (they generate few emergency calls), but they concentrate two hazards worth understanding: diesel fuel and lithium-ion batteries. Backup generator fleets are large; Northern Virginia alone hosts more than 4,000 diesel generators, and one Amazon permit contemplates up to 10 million gallons of diesel used annually across a single campus's 173 generators. Tanks require secondary containment and spill plans under state permits.

Battery fires are rare but real. In May 2025, a battery-room fire at a Hillsboro, Oregon data center burned for hours; no one was hurt, but the X platform went down worldwide the next day. Firefighter organizations warn that lithium-ion fires behave differently from ordinary fires, resist water, and occur inside massive, security-controlled buildings that crews may never have walked.

The readiness question is answerable with money and planning. Fire codes govern battery room separation and suppression, and fire marshals can require pre-incident planning. Some developers fund readiness directly: Amazon's $1.5 million partnership with Hamlet, North Carolina paid for a fire substation, two trucks, equipment, and two years of staffing, cutting response times by 6-7 minutes and reportedly lowering every homeowner's insurance rating class. The lesson: these commitments happen when communities ask before approval, not after.

How to verify: ask your fire chief whether the operator has shared a hazardous-materials inventory and pre-incident plan, and whether responder funding and training are written conditions of approval. Diesel storage and generator counts are public in state air-permit files.

environment.title: Generators, Renewable Claims, and the Land Itself: The Environmental Ledger
paragraphs: The biggest local air issue is the backup generator fleet. Diesel generators emit nitrogen oxides, fine particulates, and air toxics, but under EPA rules they may only run about 100 hours a year for testing and maintenance (unlimited in true emergencies), so a compliant facility's normal-year emissions are modest. The risks are at the edges: Virginia's legislative research modeled a worst case where the region's thousands of generators could emit 9,000 tons of NOx a year (half the region's typical total), and in Memphis, xAI is being sued for running 33 gas turbines allegedly without any Clean Air Act permits, projected at 2,507 tons of NOx annually next to neighborhoods already failing smog standards.

Be skeptical of '100% renewable' claims. Most rest on market-based accounting: the company buys renewable certificates or contracts equal to its annual usage somewhere, while the building actually runs on the local grid mix, including gas at night. Location-based accounting, which counts the real grid, usually shows higher emissions, which is why independent researchers and the GHG Protocol are pushing hourly '24/7 carbon-free' matching as the honest standard. Ask for both numbers.

Land and water impacts are measured, not theoretical. In West Virginia, state inspectors issued repeated sediment-control violations at one campus after runoff reached an Ohio River tributary and flooded neighbors' garages, while a proposed Google campus would eliminate 34+ acres of wetlands and affect over 45,000 feet of streams with nine protected species at risk. Campus lighting is also a documented issue (residents near Meta's Louisiana site describe night skies 'lit up like New York City'), though DarkSky International says shielded fixtures, warm color temperatures, and curfew dimming can largely solve it.

How to verify: generator permits, run-hour reports, stormwater permits, and violation notices are all public records at your state environmental agency; wetland impacts appear in Army Corps permit files; and you can ask any operator for facility-specific location-based emissions and a lighting plan meeting DarkSky standards.
